content: Phenoxymethylpenicillin, commonly referred to as penicillin V, is a penicillin-class antibiotic that is effective when administered orally. It demonstrates reduced activity against Gram-negative bacteria compared to benzylpenicillin (penicillin G). However, phenoxymethylpenicillin is more stable in acidic environments than benzylpenicillin, which enables its oral administration. This antibiotic exerts a bactericidal effect on penicillin-sensitive microorganisms during their active multiplication phase. Its mechanism of action involves the inhibition of cell-wall peptidoglycan biosynthesis, which is essential for bacterial cell wall integrity. However, it is ineffective against beta-lactamase-producing bacteria, which include many strains of Staphylococci. Phenoxymethylpenicillin exhibits a spectrum of antimicrobial activity against Gram-positive bacteria that is comparable to benzylpenicillin, although it is significantly less effective against Gram-negative bacteria. It is particularly active in vitro against non-penicillinase-producing strains of Staphylococci, Streptococci (groups A, C, G, H, L, and M), and Pneumococci. Other organisms sensitive to penicillin V in vitro include Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Bacillus anthracis, Clostridia, Actinomyces bovis, Streptobacillus moniliformis, Listeria monocytogenes, Leptospira, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Additionally, Treponema pallidum, the causative agent of syphilis, is highly sensitive to this antibiotic.
